question: Which of the following wires will have the least resistance if all are made of the same material?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Short and thick wire**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Resistance** of a conductor depends on its physical dimensions and the nature of the material. According to the laws of resistance, the resistance (**R**) of a wire is **directly proportional** to its **length** (**L**). This means a **short wire** will offer **less resistance** compared to a long wire of the same material.
 
• Resistance is **inversely proportional** to the **cross-sectional area** (**A**) of the conductor. A **thick wire** has a **larger cross-sectional area**, which allows **electrons** to flow more easily, thereby resulting in **lower resistance**.
 
• Combining these factors, the formula for resistance is **R = ρ (L/A)**, where **ρ (rho)** is the **electrical resistivity** of the material. To achieve the **least resistance**, the numerator (**L**) should be as **small** as possible and the denominator (**A**) should be as **large** as possible.
 
• Therefore, a **short and thick wire** satisfies both conditions for **minimum resistance**. ***Hence, statement A is correct.***
 
• Conversely, a **long and thin wire** would have the **highest resistance** because it has a **greater length** and a **smaller area**. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Electrical Resistivity (ρ):**

 
 
• It is a **fundamental property** of a material that quantifies how strongly it resists or conducts **electric current**.
 
• The **SI unit** of resistivity is the **Ohm-metre (Ω⋅m)**.
 
• Materials like **Silver**, **Copper**, and **Aluminium** have very **low resistivity**, making them **excellent conductors** for **electrical wiring**.
 
 
 
• **Ohm's Law:**
 
 
• Proposed by **Georg Simon Ohm** in **1827**, it states that the **current (I)** through a conductor between two points is **directly proportional** to the **voltage (V)** across the two points, provided **temperature** remains constant.
 
• The relationship is expressed as **V = IR**, where **R** is the **Resistance**.
 
• The **SI unit** of resistance is the **Ohm (Ω)**.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Resistance:**
 
 
• **Nature of Material:** Different materials have different densities of **free electrons**. For example, **Nichrome** has higher resistance than **Copper** and is used in **heating elements**.
 
• **Temperature:** For **pure metals**, resistance **increases** with an **increase in temperature** because the **thermal vibrations** of atoms interfere with the flow of **electrons**.
 
• **Dimensions:** As discussed, **length** and **thickness (diameter)** are primary physical factors.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Applications of Low Resistance Wires:** **Thick copper wires** are used in **power transmission lines** and **heavy-duty appliances** like **air conditioners** to minimize **energy loss** due to **Joule heating (H = I²Rt)**.
 
• **Applications of High Resistance Wires:** **Thin wires** made of alloys like **Tungsten** are used in **incandescent bulbs** because their **high resistance** generates enough **heat** to produce **light**.
 
• **Numerical Value Context:** If the **length** of a wire is **doubled**, its **resistance doubles**. If the **radius** of a wire is **doubled**, the **area increases fourfold**, which causes the **resistance to decrease to one-fourth** of its original value.
 
• In the context of **India**, the **Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)** sets guidelines for the **gauge (thickness)** and **quality** of wiring used in **residential and industrial buildings** to ensure safety and **efficiency**.
